title: Ancient Roman Calendar Notation
intro: Roman writers often named a date by counting backward from the Kalends, Nones or Ides, rather than numbering the day forward through a month.
summary: A Roman-style way of saying a date, applied here to the Julian calendar's familiar month and day structure.
origin: The Kalends marked the first day of the month; Nones and Ides were additional traditional reference dates. The Ides of March is a famous example.
structure: The program uses proleptic Julian dates, then renders traditional Roman month landmarks and inclusive backward counting.
pattern_note: The number of days counted is inclusive: the destination landmark is counted as one. Nones and Ides fall later in March, May, July and October.
history: This naming convention reflects Roman public and civic practice and survives in many Latin quotations. Roman month and leap-day reckoning had a longer, more complicated history.
example: 15 March is the Ides of March. The day before the Ides may be described as pridie Idus Martias in the traditional style.
limits: This provider uses Roman names over a mathematically extended Julian calendar. It is not a reconstruction of all pre-Julian Roman intercalations or early regnal chronology.
